title: Revisiting partition priming in judgement under uncertainty

source.title: Revisiting partition priming in judgement under uncertainty: replication and extension Registered Report of Fox and Rottenstreich (2003)

studies.title: Study 1a · Three probability judgments
studies.description: Weather, sport and stock judgments in the shared Prolific survey.

studies.title: Study 1b · Weekday or weekend
studies.description: A reversed prediction tested in the same Prolific participants.

studies.title: Study 3 · Job offer
studies.description: A job-offer probability judgment with background information, in the same Prolific survey.

studies.title: Study 4 · Financial choice
studies.description: A binary choice about the stock scenario in the same Prolific survey.

nodes.title: Can wording change a probability judgment?

fields.label: Research question
fields.value: When a question describes the same uncertain event in different ways, does the wording change which possibilities people compare and the probability they assign? The registered report revisits the effect across numerical judgments and a financial choice.

fields.label: Ignorance priors
fields.value: With little relevant information, people may begin by assigning equal chances to possibilities they see as comparable. Binary case wording suggests two outcomes. Class wording calls attention to a larger set of possibilities.

fields.label: Scope of replication
fields.value: Four named studies from Fox and Rottenstreich (2003) were combined into one survey. The authors left the original Study 2 out because its classroom methods, procedure and results were scarcely described.

fields.label: Study 1a · Weather, sport and stocks
fields.value: Case wording (1/2) was expected to produce higher event probabilities than class wording (1/7 for weather and sport, 1/30 for stocks).

fields.label: Study 1b · Weekday warmth
fields.value: The prediction reverses: class wording enumerates five weekdays out of seven and was expected to yield higher ratings than binary case wording (1/2).

fields.label: Study 3 · Job offer
fields.value: Case wording was expected to produce higher ratings for a candidate’s job offer (case prior 1/2, class prior 1/10) even when people can use information about the candidate.

fields.label: Study 4 · Riskier financial choice
fields.value: Participants under case wording were expected to choose the uncertain $50 option more often than those under class wording. The two primes suggest priors of 1/2 and 1/30 for the same uncertain option.

fields.label: Exploratory complements
fields.value: The complementary-event analyses were exploratory, without specific predictions. The task-order test for Study 4 was planned; the parallel order analysis for Study 1a Item 3 was added after data collection.

nodes.title: One sample, two wordings, six scenario pages

fields.label: Between people
fields.value: Each participant was randomly assigned to case or class wording for the entire survey. The underlying target event was held constant across wordings. The analyzed groups were 300 case and 303 class.

fields.label: Within each person
fields.value: Everyone received six randomly ordered pages: three Study 1a items, one Study 1b item, one Study 3 item and one Study 4 choice. The 2003 paper used separate samples for these studies.

fields.label: Question order within a page
fields.value: Every probability scenario paired a happen rating with a not-happen rating. The procedure section and original Qualtrics order place happen first. The design section separately describes the order of the two questions as randomized.

fields.label: Sample and exclusions
fields.value: 603 US participants completed the survey, including 30 pretest participants. Of 707 people who began, 104 stopped at consent or verification. The authors kept all completers and classified no cases as outliers.

fields.label: Compensation
fields.value: Pretest participants received £0.95 and the remaining participants received a fixed £1.05. The Study 4 dollar options were scenario choices.

fields.label: Prolific screening
fields.value: The main paper and the supplement’s recruitment list report 100–10,000 prior submissions. Another line in the supplement reports 5,000–100,000 approved submissions. The applied count criterion needs confirmation.

fields.label: Study 1a · Three judgments
fields.value: The scenarios ask about the hottest day at O’Hare Airport, the University of Michigan winning a women’s lacrosse scoring title, and IBM outperforming the other Dow Jones stocks. The replication updated the sport and stock stimuli.

fields.label: Study 1b · A weekday versus the weekend
fields.value: The target event is that the warmest day next week is a weekday, where the class framing counts five of the seven days.

fields.label: Study 3 · A job offer
fields.value: Participants learned ACME planned 10 job offers for 100 applicants. They read a recommendation excerpt about K.T. and judged whether K.T. would receive an offer.

fields.label: Study 4 · A stock-linked choice
fields.value: The options are a certain $10 and a $50 payment contingent on IBM outperforming every other Dow Jones stock. The two options appeared in randomized order.

fields.label: Survey sequence
fields.value: Participants consented and answered screening questions, received one framing condition, completed all six scenarios in randomized order, and answered follow-up and demographic questions.

fields.label: Manipulation
fields.value: Case wording asks whether a specified event will occur. Class wording locates the same event in a set of alternatives.

fields.label: Probability judgments
fields.value: Participants entered 0–100% for each happen and not-happen prompt. They could enter both values freely. In exploratory analyses the authors compared the happen rating with the reverse-coded complement (100% minus the not-happen rating).

fields.label: Financial choice
fields.value: The outcome was which option the participant chose. It was recorded as a binary choice without asking for a numerical probability.

fields.label: Probability ratings
fields.value: For the five happen questions, the authors compared the two conditions with Mann–Whitney U and Welch’s t-tests. Chi-squared tests compared the share of responses within five percentage points of the case or class prior.

fields.label: How replication success was decided
fields.value: The preregistration defined success as three or four of the four studies showing a signal in the expected direction. After seeing the results, the authors adopted a two-of-three rule for Study 1a and designated Mann–Whitney as the primary test for its rating outcomes.

fields.label: Choice comparison
fields.value: Study 4 compared the proportion choosing the contingent option across conditions using a two-proportion z-test.

fields.label: Item 1 · Weather
fields.value: Mean happen estimates were 31.93% (case) and 26.66% (class). Both the Mann–Whitney test (p = .013) and Welch test (p = .003) supported the expected direction. Both prior-alignment comparisons supported the prediction.

fields.label: Item 2 · Sports
fields.value: Means were 27.74% and 25.06%. Mann–Whitney supported a difference (p = .021); Welch did not (p = .075). Class-prior alignment supported the prediction; case-prior alignment did not.

fields.label: Item 3 · IBM stock
fields.value: Means were 19.77% and 17.97%. Neither the Mann–Whitney (p = .092) nor the Welch test (p = .304) supported the overall effect; neither prior-alignment comparison supported it.

fields.label: Complementary judgments
fields.value: The not-happen analyses supported a weather difference in both tests. For sports, the narrative describes Mann–Whitney support, but Table 15 prints p = .400 alongside a significance mark. The Welch test gives p = .133. The stock item had no clear between-condition difference.

fields.label: Stock question order
fields.value: The exploratory relative-order ANOVA found no clear evidence of an order effect or an order-by-framing interaction. When the stock item appeared first, the conditional Mann–Whitney comparison met the planned .005 threshold (p = .004) and Welch did not (p = .047). Both tests were inconclusive when another item appeared first.

fields.label: Event probabilities
fields.value: The mean happen rating was 56.83% under case wording and 66.91% under class wording, the predicted reverse direction. Mann–Whitney and Welch both gave p < .001. Both prior-alignment comparisons supported the prediction.

fields.label: Complementary judgment
fields.value: The mean not-happen ratings reversed that pattern: 45.20% in case and 32.58% in class. The exploratory Mann–Whitney and Welch comparisons both gave p < .001.

fields.label: Event probabilities
fields.value: The mean happen rating was 59.93% under case wording and 47.53% under class wording. Mann–Whitney and Welch both gave p < .001. The authors found support for class-prior alignment and no clear evidence for case-prior alignment.

fields.label: Complementary judgment
fields.value: The mean not-happen rating was 40.95% in case and 50.47% in class. The exploratory Mann–Whitney and Welch comparisons both gave p < .001.

fields.label: Share choosing the uncertain option
fields.value: The contingent $50 option was chosen by 21.00% of case-framed participants and 23.76% of class-framed participants. The two-proportion test gave p = .415. The result provided no clear support for the predicted greater risk-taking under case wording.

fields.label: Did task order affect choice?
fields.value: The logistic model provided no clear evidence for an effect of task order, framing or their interaction on the choice of the uncertain option.

nodes.title: What the exploratory complement tests showed

fields.label: Across the five estimation scenarios
fields.value: The mixed ANOVA found differences across scenarios, a scenario-by-framing interaction and an evaluation-type difference. It found no clear overall framing effect or three-way interaction.

fields.label: Exception to complementary consistency
fields.value: In class framing for the IBM stock item, mean happen was 17.97%, while the mean of 100 minus not-happen was 24.46% (post hoc p < .001). This was the only highlighted pair with clear evidence of a difference.

fields.label: Mostly successful, with variation by scenario
fields.value: After analysis the authors decided to use Mann–Whitney as the core test and to count Study 1a as supported if two of its three items showed the expected effect. Under those decisions, they counted Study 1a as supported and found support for Studies 1b and 3. The IBM stock judgment and Study 4 financial choice showed no consistent support. Most effects were weaker than those reported in the original paper.

fields.label: Replicating across settings
fields.value: The replication combined four originally separate studies, updated stimuli and sampled adults through Prolific. The authors describe the replication as close to far, and note that their selected scenarios cover a limited part of the evidence.

issues.title: Original paired-question order unspecified
issues.reason: The replication paper says the 2003 article did not specify whether pairs appeared together or the six questions were counterbalanced.
issues.impact: The 2025 survey establishes its own order. The original procedure remains uncertain.
issues.suggestedAction: Consult the original survey or author records if the 2003 order is needed.

issues.title: Analysis scripts outside this package
issues.reason: The paper points to OSF scripts, which were outside the approved staged inputs.
issues.impact: This Program describes reported results. It does not establish raw-data or analysis-code reproduction.
issues.suggestedAction: Use the authors’ OSF project for an approved code review.

issues.title: Two descriptions of question order
issues.reason: The design section describes happen/not-happen order as randomized, while the procedure section and the administered survey use fixed order within each page.
issues.impact: The procedure description governs the 2025 instrument summary.
issues.suggestedAction: Read the original QSF flow and scenario blocks if auditing the implementation.

issues.title: Submission thresholds differ across sources
issues.reason: The main Methods and the supplement’s filter list give 100–10,000 submissions, but an additional line of the supplement gives 5,000–100,000.
issues.suggestedAction: Confirm the filters used for this Prolific recruitment with the authors or original recruitment record.

issues.title: Sports complement p-value is inconsistent
issues.reason: Table 15 prints p = .400 with a significance mark and the narrative describes Mann–Whitney support.
issues.impact: The exact reported sports complement significance is unresolved.
issues.suggestedAction: Check the authors’ analysis output or request a correction.
